name: Atal Bihari Vajpayee
role: Prime Minister of India (1996, 1998-2004); founding BJP president (1980); External Affairs Minister (1977-79)
summary: Vajpayee was a Hindu-nationalist parliamentarian who combined cultural nationalism with a conciliatory, coalition-minded style. As prime minister he tested nuclear weapons, pursued talks with Pakistan, privatised public enterprises and kept contentious BJP aims (Ram temple, Article 370, a uniform civil code) out of the coalition agenda. He opposed the Emergency, defended parliamentary democracy and secularism as he defined them, and was criticised for his handling of the 2002 Gujarat violence.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Mixed: his government privatised and liberalised, but the 1998 manifesto he led says the state continues to manage and protect the economy even in a liberalised regime and rejects leaving things to a hidden hand.

public-ownership.rationale: His governments' record is disinvestment and privatisation: a Department of Disinvestment (1999) upgraded to a Ministry (2001), sales of VSNL, BALCO, Hindustan Zinc and others, and a manifesto pledge to disinvest non-strategic PSUs and bring private firms into oil, coal and telecom. He kept some strategic public enterprises, so not -2.

cut-welfare.rationale: The manifesto promises to trim subsidies except those that benefit weaker sections, and his government ran Antyodaya Anna Yojana for the poorest families, which he described in 2003 as a very large food-security programme. No statement that welfare creates dependency.

strong-leader.rationale: He was jailed in the 1975-77 Emergency, framed the issue in 1969 as democracy versus totalitarianism, and told the UN in 1977 that measures were being devised so freedoms could never again be smothered. He governed through coalition and left office after losing votes in 1996, 1999 and 2004.

empower-police-military.rationale: The manifesto promises modern arms for police, a free hand for security forces against insurgency and a strengthened armed forces; in 1998 he said India must modernise its forces.

decide-locally.rationale: The manifesto pledges to implement the Sarkaria Commission, give states a larger tax share and greater functional autonomy, and strengthen panchayats; his 2003 speech stresses cooperative relations with states of different parties. No statement that decisions should be local wherever possible.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: He repeatedly stated cultural nationalism: India as an ancient nation to be made virile, a call to resist an 'imported' video culture (1968, 1984 sessions), and the manifesto he led calls cultural heritage the core of its nationalism.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: In 1977 he said the UN should become a 'parliament of man' and exercise its authority to extend sanctions on Rhodesia; the manifesto seeks UN reform and a Security Council seat. Dated evidence.

free-trade.rationale: Mixed: the manifesto he led argues free trade is a slogan and favours economic nationalism, while his government reduced tariffs and continued liberalisation.

nation-first.rationale: The manifesto defines Swadeshi as 'India first', and he ordered the 1998 nuclear tests despite expected sanctions; he also pursued dialogue with Pakistan and engagement with the US and China.

limit-growth.rationale: The 1998 manifesto sets a target of sustained 8 to 9 per cent growth and proposes speeding infrastructure clearances; he did not argue for limiting growth.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The manifesto promises to restart and expand the stalled nuclear power programme, and in 1977 he opposed measures that block peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

revolution-justified.rationale: No recorded position found in a source above the tertiary tier (encyclopedia or quotation compilation only).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Contested: the 1998 manifesto criticises misguided tariff reductions, promises anti-dumping machinery and protection of national industry during a seven-to-ten-year transition, but his government's record was continued liberalisation.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Contested: the manifesto says governments actively manage and protect their economies and national industry, and his government led the state-planned highway network (Golden Quadrilateral), but he also privatised enterprises; no statement on steering investment to strategic industries as such.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The manifesto stresses strengthening small-scale, tiny and cottage units and small farmers, within a market framework; it does not state a general principle that property should be widely spread.

one-party-rule.rationale: No recorded position found in a source above the tertiary tier (encyclopedia or quotation compilation only).

democracy-best.rationale: He said democracy is necessary for national unity and safe so long as voters stay vigilant (1998), resigned in 1996 rather than seek a majority by other means, and left office after losing in 2004.

right-to-secede.rationale: In 2003 he said advocates of self-determination for Kashmir would not be allowed to succeed; the manifesto calls for abrogating Article 370 and keeps Kashmir integral, and his government fought the Kargil war over the Line of Control.

political-violence-never.rationale: He condemned terrorism in all forms (2001) and said of the 1992 Babri demolition that it should not have happened; he did not address insurrection or revolutionary violence as a general principle.

separate-church-state.rationale: Mixed: he defined a secular state as one that does not identify with any mode of worship and holds the balance among sects, yet rejected reading secularism as a state indifferent to dharma; not a call for strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In 1998 he said nobody had asked to declare Hindu religion the state religion, and he defended India's secular constitutional order in 1998 and 2002 speeches; he never advocated scripture-based law.

military-superiority.rationale: The manifesto commits to expanding India's power projection, building the Agni missile series and neutralising rivals' advanced systems, and he said in 1998 India must modernise its forces.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He described India as a diverse nation whose diversity 'needs to be preserved' (1968) and said diversity is strength (2000), while also calling India a Hindu nation in cultural terms; he did not call for ethnic homogeneity.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The manifesto promises to revive the faith that nature is sacred and to include environment studies in curricula.

direct-action.rationale: Inferred: he chose elections, coalition-building and parliamentary debate and stated in 1998 that democracy needs vigilant voters.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: No recorded position found in a source above the tertiary tier (encyclopedia or quotation compilation only).

total-state.rationale: In 1969 he identified totalitarianism as the thing to be resisted and the 1998 manifesto describes institutions as limited pillars; he resisted the Emergency.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In 1977 he said India seeks friendship with all and dominance over none, and in 1959 he condemned Chinese expansionism as new imperialism.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The manifesto promises worker participation from the shopfloor to the boardroom; never enacted in his term, and it is a party platform.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His government enacted the FRBM Act 2003 setting statutory limits on revenue and fiscal deficits, and the manifesto promised to cut non-productive expenditure. Enacted by his government rather than stated by him personally, so medium.

national-self-determination.rationale: He supported independence for Algeria and Tibet in 1959 and the Palestinians' return and rights in 1977, but denied self-determination to Kashmir in 2003, a region of his own state.

force-without-un.rationale: Inferred: in July 2003 his government declined a US request to send troops to Iraq without an explicit UN mandate; he fought no war abroad.

class-collaboration.rationale: The manifesto commits to make labour an 'equal and proud partner' in national progress, and he spoke at BJP sessions of bridging the gap between capital and labour.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: He urged conservation of heritage in 2003 and the manifesto commits to preserving and projecting cultural heritage and traditional knowledge.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: At the UN in 1977 he said apartheid must go, called it a blot on humanity and said all forms of racialism must be eradicated root and branch.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The manifesto promises more coal production and private participation in oil extraction and refining and in coal mining.

proportional-representation.rationale: Mixed: he said in 1998 the number of parties should be reduced for stability, while the manifesto only promises to examine a list or mixed electoral system.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In 2002 he said a ruler should not discriminate among subjects on caste, creed or religion, and in 1977 called for all racialism to be eradicated. The record on Gujarat is contested, so not high.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Mixed: the 1998 manifesto commits to a Uniform Civil Code formulated by the Law Commission, but the NDA agenda his government governed by omitted it and it was not pursued.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Mixed: he called for a national debate on conversions in the late 1990s, then withdrew from it after reaction; in 2002 he said faith cannot be spread by the sword. No law restricting conversion was proposed by his government.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: The 1998 manifesto pledges a total ban on slaughter of cows and their progeny, but his government did not legislate one and the issue was left out of the coalition agenda.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Inferred: in 1977 he called the post-Emergency election a 'magnificent assertion of the human spirit' and spoke of democracy and basic rights being restored.

separated-powers.rationale: The 1998 manifesto says democracy's strength rests on the executive, legislature and judiciary as three pillars needing reform and strengthening.

priority-to-poor.rationale: His 2003 speech presented the Antyodaya Anna Yojana for the poorest as a major priority and spoke of faster poverty reduction, and the manifesto's vision begins with freedom from hunger and unemployment; he did not say the poor must come first in all law.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: No recorded position found in a source above the tertiary tier (encyclopedia or quotation compilation only).

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He was imprisoned in the 1975-77 Emergency and at the UN in 1977 welcomed restoration of basic rights; his government's POTA (2002), however, extended detention and evidence powers, so not -2.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Inferred: he described non-alignment in 1977 as a projection of sovereignty, 'freedom' rather than neutrality, and India joined no military alliance under him.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: He said in 1998 that social and economic justice should be achieved within the framework of democracy, and called democracy necessary for national unity.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: In 1977 he argued that resource and technology transfers to developing countries were insufficient and that rich nations should make a significant flow; a dated position from his time as foreign minister.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: His government conducted the May 1998 Pokhran-II tests, and his 27 May 1998 statement to Parliament presented the weapons as India's self-defence deterrent, refusing the NPT and CTBT as then framed.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Mixed: he pursued a settlement with Pakistan at Lahore (1999) and Agra (2001), saying mindsets and historical baggage must change, while holding Kashmir as integral and recognising Tibet as part of China in 2003.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Mixed: in 1977 he said Israeli-occupied territories must be vacated and demanded no recognition, but in 2003 he recognised Tibet as part of China despite his 1959 stance.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: His government continued counter-insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir while offering talks; he said separatists will not succeed, but he did not describe force as the answer to secession in so many words.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Mixed: his government rejected the 2000 Jammu and Kashmir autonomy resolution and the manifesto calls for abrogating Article 370, but he spoke of alternatives to the beaten track on Kashmir.

refugee-return.rationale: In 1977 he said the Palestinians must be able to exercise their inalienable right to return to their land.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: His government pushed a 33 per cent reservation for women in legislatures, and in 2003 floated double-member seats to get it passed; that is below equal or near-equal representation.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The manifesto explicitly rejects economic isolationism while pursuing 'India first' (Swadeshi) and calibrated globalisation; no colonial bloc concept.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: No recorded position found in a source above the tertiary tier (encyclopedia or quotation compilation only).

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: In 1959 he backed Algerian and Tibetan independence and opposed imperial rule, and in 1977 he rejected dominance over others.

delink-world-market.rationale: His government kept integrating with the world economy (investment promotion, WTO engagement) and the manifesto states the aim is calibrated integration, 'not economic isolationism'.

notes: Attributed primary texts could not be downloaded in full: the Parliament digital library (eparlib) and PIB archives refused connections, so confidence-vote speeches and his collected speeches were not searched; the 1998 manifesto is a party document he fronted, and where it conflicts with his government's record (UCC, Article 370, cow slaughter, tariffs) the answer is mixed. His 1977 UN speech says India would not build nuclear weapons, but his later 1998 position (tests and a weaponised deterrent) governs. Raj dharma remark of April 2002 and a Goa speech passage on Muslims remain contested.
